scope.line: I led the UI competency and a product squad inside a design function that grew to twenty-four.
scope.detail: Within the design org I owned the UI competency and ran design for an HRx squad. Title moved from Lead UI Designer to Dy. Design Manager.

timeline.head: Two designers. Zero process.
timeline.body: Reviews were vibes-based. “Does this look okay?” “Yeah… I think so?” Feedback was nodding until the silence ended. Nobody wanted to be the bad guy.

timeline.head: Doubled the team. Chaos doubled faster.
timeline.body: Onboarding was a Google Doc and a prayer. Three designers redesigning the same component, and none of them knew.
timeline.note: “Doubled” is the word in the source; 4 is my reading of it, not a counted figure.

timeline.head: Started building rituals. Accidentally.
timeline.body: The first structured critique happened because I got frustrated in a meeting. Someone wrote it down. We did it again. Then it was a Thing.
timeline.note: No headcount is recorded for 2021. The dot is positioned between the 2020 and 2022 figures and is illustrative.

timeline.head: Ten designers. Culture became visible.
timeline.body: Juniors started running sessions. Seniors started saying “you’re right.” Design presented directly to leadership. I started sitting in the back row.

timeline.head: Twenty-four designers. And the award.
timeline.body: Fifteen UX and nine UI, split across two competencies. I held the UI side. In the same year the team won Best Team at AOP.
timeline.note: 15 UX + 9 UI counted off the org chart in the DesignOps Review of 17 Aug 2023.

timeline.head: Reshaped around squads.
timeline.body: A January roster puts twenty-one in seat and twenty-three planned: product-embedded designers, a central floating team, interns, and single owners for the design system and the AI work.
timeline.note: Jan’25 column in Revised_Titles.xlsx: 21 current, 23 planned, interns included.

squads.intro: By 2023 the function was two competencies. By 2025 it was a hybrid: designers embedded in product squads, with a central team holding the craft.

groups.name: Product-specific teams
groups.note: embedded in a squad for 3–6 months

squads.lines_note: The four product lines the squads were drawn around.

model_objectives.label: Design Team 2.0
items: Deep product knowledge, instead of servicing tickets across everything.
Feasible solutions tied to business metrics, because the designer was in the room.
Designers lead product design independently, start to finish.
An environment where design excellence is possible, not incidental.
See the load coming, and scale up or down without guessing.
Rotation across squads every three to six months.
mechanics: Designers embedded in a product team for three to six months.
Reviewed quarterly, to rotate or scale up.
Reporting into the squad, dotted line to the UX team for mentoring.
Some dedicated to DesignOps: design system, AI products, design excellence.

rituals.name: Weekly crits
rituals.line: Silent sticky notes first. Then talk. No ambushes, and honest feedback with a name attached.

rituals.name: Design jams
rituals.line: A twenty-minute sketch sprint on a shared problem. Intern and lead drawing side by side.

rituals.name: Share & tell
rituals.line: Not what you made, but what you learned. Failures actively encouraged, and usually the most useful.

rituals.name: Chaos reviews
rituals.line: Anyone could call one. “I’m stuck, three people, fifteen minutes?” Usually solved it.

rituals.name: Know-how sessions
rituals.line: Deep dives led by the team, not by managers. The best ones ran forty-five minutes over.

rituals.name: Design lunch
rituals.line: No work allowed. Someone opened their laptop at minute twenty every single time. We allowed it.

sessions.rule: If you figured something out this week, you’re presenting it next month.
sessions.note: Presenters are named in the source. They are colleagues, so the topics are published and the names are not.

rule.line: You can disagree here. But you have to explain your thinking.

award.name: Best Team Award
award.line: Out of every team in the company, design won.
why_not: Individual brilliance or one big launch.
The design system, the metrics, the portfolio.
award.why: People across the org wanted to work with the design team. That’s it.
award.caution: The source states the award and the team’s reading of why. It does not establish that any one initiative caused it, and the page does not claim that.
phases: Two designers and startup chaos. We shipped things nobody questioned, because nobody knew how to.
Rituals formed. Crits got structured. People started saying actual things out loud.
Design started driving decisions, presenting to leadership, setting culture cross-functionally.

ladder.label: The ladder designers grew through
ladder.attrib: Career framework operated by the design organisation at Bajaj Finserv Health. Published here in sanitised form: bands and tracks only.

tracks.name: UX Design
tracks.blurb: The overall experience: usability, information architecture, content.
steps: Understands usability, accessibility, IA and interaction principles.
Wireframes and prototypes for end-to-end flows.
Defines UX guidelines for projects, aligns solutions with business and user needs, advocates for consistency.

tracks.name: UI Design
tracks.blurb: How it looks and how it responds: the visual and interaction surface.
steps: Designs screens for usability and consistency.
Defines visual standards across projects, guides teams, aligns design with business goals.

tracks.name: Product Design
tracks.blurb: Design, tech and strategy together, owning the product outcome.
steps: Understands core product design principles, tools and workflows.
High-fidelity designs aligned to user and product goals.
Reusable systems and frameworks for scalability, consistent across product workflows.
Long-term strategy, scalable frameworks, anticipating trends to create future-ready solutions.

tracks.name: Design Engineering
tracks.blurb: Design to code: front-end fundamentals, increasingly AI-assisted.
steps: Design principles plus HTML and CSS, enough to collaborate properly with developers.
Builds prototypes and components with AI tools.
Sets the direction for AI-powered design workflows across the organisation.

tracks.name: Design Management
tracks.blurb: Leading the team that does the work.
steps: Coaches and mentors to scale quality.
Mentorship programmes, frameworks for hiring, upskilling and retaining talent.

rise.name: RISE
rise.attrib: A company programme spanning Technology, Product and Design.
cycle: The competencies that matter at each band.
Rate against them, one to four, self and manager.
Turn the gap into an individual development plan.
Training and masterclasses against that plan.

principles.title: Ownership over micromanagement
principles.body: Talented people perform best when the work is genuinely theirs. I hire people I believe in, give them real ownership, and hold them to outcomes rather than to process.
principles.pull: If I’m the bottleneck, the system is broken.

principles.title: Safety to speak honestly
principles.body: The quality of a team’s work tracks how safe people feel being wrong. We built that into critique deliberately: “I don’t know yet” and “I was wrong about this” were normal sentences.

principles.title: Give the team the spotlight
principles.body: When the team can shine, I stay in the background. Credit gets attributed correctly, and designers present their own work, including to the people who sign it off.
principles.pull: If you designed it, you present it.

principles.title: Think in systems
principles.body: Whether it is one user flow or an organisation: how do the parts interact, where are the dependencies, what breaks under load. The same habit shaped the design system and the shape of the team.
principles.pull: Scale exposes weak systems. It doesn’t create them.

principles.title: Hire for slope, not position
principles.body: Where someone is today matters less than how fast they move. I look for people who can explain why they designed something, who say “I did” rather than “they told me”, and who frame the problem before solving it.
principles.pull: I don’t hire for today’s tasks. I hire for tomorrow’s judgement.

closing.head: Still building. Still learning. Still making room.
closing.body: What I learned growing this team is the thing I now work on directly: the operating layer underneath design. How work gets planned, how quality gets held, how AI changes what a design team even is. Different problem, same instinct: build the system, then get out of the way.
links: How design works, as its own practice
closing.sign: Earlier, I measured my value by how much I contributed. Scaling forced me to measure it by how little I needed to.
